title: The Hidden Cost of Climate Change: Our Brains
title_zh: 气候变化的隐性代价：我们的大脑
source_name: University of Chicago Climate — “Climate Impacts on Brain Health Are Overlooked—and Unaddressed by Policy” (26 Oct 2026)
summary_zh: 据芝加哥大学气候网站 10 月 26 日报道，发表在学术期刊《One Earth》上的一篇评论文章指出：气候变化对大脑健康（包括心理健康）的影响被严重忽视，几乎没有进入政策视野。高温会增加中风和痴呆症相关的住院人数；极端天气与创伤后应激障碍、抑郁、焦虑等有关；空气污染会引发炎症，并与痴呆、认知能力下降等相关。儿童、老人和低收入社区受到的影响尤其大。目前将近三分之二的国家气候适应政策没有提到心理健康，而重要的气候经济评估也没有把心理健康成本算进去——全球与心理健康相关的福利损失估计高达 5 万亿美元。作者建议城市设立清洁空气区、建设能降温的绿色基础设施，国家制定包含心理健康内容的气候与健康战略。文章还举例：印度艾哈迈达巴德的“高温行动计划”每年减少约 1,190 例死亡；欧盟加强空气质量措施后，2005 到 2023 年间与颗粒物污染相关的过早死亡减少了 57%。作者认为，下一步要先加强数据测量。
paragraphs: When people talk about the effects of climate change, they usually mention rising seas, failed harvests or damaged homes. However, a new commentary published in the scientific journal One Earth argues that one serious consequence is almost completely ignored: the impact on our brains.

The authors, who include psychologists and policy experts from the University of Chicago, the University of Washington and the International Neuro Climate Working Group, describe several ways in which a changing climate can harm brain health. Extreme heat is linked to more hospital admissions for stroke and dementia. Floods, storms and other disasters can lead to depression, anxiety and post-traumatic stress disorder. Air pollution causes inflammation in the body and has been connected to memory loss and cognitive decline.

These risks are not shared equally. The researchers give the example of a child growing up in a poor neighbourhood of a hot coastal city. The child breathes dirtier air, has little access to parks, cooling or good healthcare, and faces a higher chance of trauma if a disaster strikes. In other words, the damage is biological, social and psychological at the same time. Children, older adults and low-income communities are therefore the most vulnerable.

Despite this evidence, the issue rarely appears in official plans. Almost two-thirds of national climate adaptation policies do not mention mental health at all. One reason is that major studies of the economic cost of climate change usually leave mental health out, even though mental illness already causes an estimated five trillion dollars in welfare losses worldwide every year.

The authors stress that the situation is not hopeless. Cities could create clean-air zones, reduce traffic emissions and plant trees to cool down hot streets. Governments could include mental health in their national climate and health strategies. Real examples show that such policies work: a heat action plan in Ahmedabad, India, has reduced deaths by about 1,190 a year, and stronger air-quality rules in the European Union cut premature deaths linked to particle pollution by 57 percent between 2005 and 2023.
According to the researchers, the first step is better measurement. If governments understand the true cost of climate change to our minds, they will be more likely to protect them.

key_words.meaning_zh: adj. 脆弱的；易受伤害的
n. 适应；（气候）适应措施
